passages.happening:
“Is not man consigned to labor on earth? Are not his days like those of a hired hand?” (verse 1). Like a slave longing for shade, like a laborer waiting for his wages, Job has been given months of futility and nights of misery. When he lies down he asks when he will get up, and he tosses until dawn. His skin is cracked and festering.

“My days are swifter than a weaver’s shuttle; they come to an end without hope” (verse 6). “Remember that my life is but a breath. My eyes will never again see happiness” (verse 7).

The eye that sees him now will not see him again. “As a cloud vanishes and is gone, so he who goes down to Sheol does not come back up. He never returns to his house; his place remembers him no more” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
Job's pictures come from ordinary working life. The hired hand worked for a daily wage, and Israel's law required that he be paid before sunset because he depended on it (Deuteronomy 24:14-15). The slave had no wage at all, only the hope of shade at the end of the day. Job's months feel like that: work with no reward and no end.

The weaver's shuttle carried the thread back and forth across the loom, flying fast, and a thread cut from the loom was a common ancient picture of a life ended.

Sheol was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, where all the dead went, pictured as a land of no return. It is not the later idea of hell as a place of punishment. For Job it means the end of return, work and remembrance, which is why he wants God to act now.

Notice the word breath in verse 7. Job's life seems to him brief and weightless. He will say it again in verse 16.
passages.later: A psalm says the same of every human life: “Truly each man at his best exists as but a breath” (Psalm 39:5).
passages.asks: Job's nights were long and his days flew. Ask whether you have known that strange mix of time, and who stayed with you in it. And ask who near you is lying awake tonight.

passages.t: What is man, that You watch him so?
passages.happening:
“Therefore I will not restrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul” (verse 11). Now Job speaks to God.

“Am I the sea, or the monster of the deep, that You must keep me under guard?” (verse 12). When he hopes his bed will comfort him, God frightens him with dreams and visions, so that he would rather die than live in his body. “I loathe my life! I would not live forever. Leave me alone, for my days are but a breath” (verse 16).

“What is man that You should exalt him, that You should set Your heart upon him, that You attend to him every morning, and test him every moment?” (verses 17-18). Will God never look away long enough for him to swallow? “If I have sinned, what have I done to You, O watcher of mankind? Why have You made me Your target” (verse 20). “Why do You not pardon my transgression and take away my iniquity? For soon I will lie down in the dust; You will seek me, but I will be no more” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
Verse 11 is the hinge. Until now Job has spoken about God. From here he speaks to him, as You, and from now on the book's argument is between Job and God as well as between Job and his friends.

Verse 12 draws on pictures shared across the region. In texts from Ugarit, on the Syrian coast, the storm god fights Yam, the Sea, and monsters of the deep, and Israel's poets sometimes used such images for the LORD's rule over every rebellious power. Job asks whether he is such a threat that God must set a guard over him.

Verses 17 and 18 turn Psalm 8 inside out. That psalm marvels that God is mindful of human beings. Job asks the same question with bitter irony. God's attention, which should comfort him, feels like an inspector's audit. The verb for attend, paqad, can mean a gracious visit or an inspection.

His last question is one of the most honest in the book. If he has sinned, why not simply forgive him, before it is too late?
passages.later: The psalm Job turns inside out says it with wonder: “what is man that You are mindful of him, or the son of man that You care for him?” (Psalm 8:4). And another psalm prays as Job does: “Turn Your gaze away from me, that I may again be cheered before I depart and am no more” (Psalm 39:13).
passages.hard:
Is Job sinning when he speaks to God this way?

Job accuses God of guarding him like an enemy and refusing to look away. Many readers find this shocking, and the friends think it dangerous talk. Yet the book frames Job's words with care. At the end God tells Eliphaz that the friends have not spoken rightly about him, as Job has (42:7). Interpreters read that verdict in different ways. Some think God approves Job's honesty and his refusal to pretend, while not endorsing every accusation; God does rebuke Job's words without knowledge in chapters 38 to 41, and Job takes them back (42:6). Others stress that Job, unlike his friends, kept speaking to God and not only about him. Either way, the book does not treat lament as unbelief. Job's protest assumes that God is real, that he is just, and that he is the one to whom Job must speak.

When Job says he would rather die than live in his body (verse 15), the book records his anguish without recommending it. It is a cry in the dark, not the book's counsel.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Job told God exactly how his attention felt. Ask whether you have ever been that honest in prayer. And ask whether you believe God would rather hear your complaint than your silence.
